StringWithMarkup.String: Trimethoxysilane's production and use as an organic coupling agent, adhesive and binding agent, surface activating agent, and as an intermediate in the industrial production of organosilanes such as trimethoxysilylpropyl methacrylate may result in its release to the environment through various waste streams. If released to air, a vapor pressure of 76 mm Hg at 25 °C indicates trimethoxysilane will exist solely in the vapor phase in the atmosphere. Vapor-phase trimethoxysilane will be degraded in the atmosphere by reaction with photochemically-produced hydroxyl radicals; the half-life for this reaction in air is estimated to be 6.4 days, however, hydrolysis in air is estimated to occur faster with a half life of 0.05 hours (3 min). Trimethoxysilane does not contain chromophores that absorb at wavelengths >290 nm and, therefore, is not expected to be susceptible to direct photolysis by sunlight. If released to soil, trimethoxysilane is expected to have moderate mobility based upon an estimated Koc of 220; however, it is unlikely to persist in the environment due to the potential for hydrolysis in the presence of moisture in air. Biodegradation, bioconcentration and volatilization are not important fate processes since hydrolysis occurs rapidly. If released into water, trimethoxysilane will hydrolyze rapidly and therefore is not expected to adsorb to suspended solids and sediments. The hydrolytic half-life of trimethoxysilane in water is 0.3 minutes at 2 degrees C, pH 7.0, and 0.2 min at pH 9.0 and pH 4.0. Occupational exposure to trimethoxysilane may occur through dermal contact or inhalation of this compound at workplaces where trimethoxysilane is produced or used. Due to the reactive nature of this compound, it is produced and used as a site-limited intermediate in closed systems, limiting the potential for exposure. Exposure to trimethoxysilane among the general population is not expected due to the rapid hydrolysis when exposed to moisture in the environment; limited exposure may occur during the use of commercial products containing this compound. Final products generally contain less than 0.001 percent trimethoxysilane but may contain up to 0.2 percent. (SRC)

Section.Description: Sorption to soils and sediments is an important factor on the transport and fate of organic contaminants in the environment.  The soil/water adsorption coefficient, also known as solid-water distribution coefficient (Kd), measures the amount of chemical substance adsorbed onto soil per amount of water.  Since adsorption occurs predominantly by partition into the soil organic matter, it is more useful to normalize the Kd value to the organic carbon content of a soil and express the distribution coefficient in Koc (organic carbon normalized distribution coefficient).  The greater the Kd (or Koc) value, the less likely a chemical will leach or contribute to runoff.  A very high value means it is strongly adsorbed onto soil and organic matter and does not move throughout the soil.
